unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 1 of your Year 8 English course at Ehel Academy. The theme is languages and communication: how ideas travel, how rumours outrun facts, and how careful readers and listeners separate the two. You will read two information texts about how rumours spread and how to check them, then follow Amal and Nora through the story Whispers Beyond the Gate as a hoax flyer sweeps their harbour city. The grammar focus covers contrast conjunctions (although, while, whereas), -ing forms as subjects and objects, the present continuous, abstract nouns, reported speech, conditionals, connectives and multi-word verbs. Along the way you will learn thirty-one new words, write a contrast paragraph and an opinion essay, and argue a case aloud for five to six minutes.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise a cohesive multi-paragraph response. Present, defend, reflect and complete the quiz.

readings.title: The Speed of a Whisper: How Rumours Travel
readings.setting: A modern harbour city and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
A rumour is a story that runs ahead of its facts. It moves from friend to friend and from screen to screen, changing a little with every telling. The version that reaches the last listener may barely resemble the truth that started it. Understanding how rumours travel is one of the most useful skills a Year 8 student can learn, because the channels that carry useful knowledge carry misinformation just as smoothly.
Why do rumours move so fast? The first reason is excitement. Dramatic news produces a small thrill, and passing it on lets the messenger share that thrill. Some people forward every alarming message with zeal, proud to be first with the drama. The second reason is belonging. Agreeing with a rumour feels like joining a team, and questioning it can feel like letting the team down. The third reason is speed itself. A message that once needed a day to cross a town now crosses a continent in seconds, long before anyone has checked a single fact. Forwarding takes one tap, whereas checking takes ten patient minutes, and the tap usually wins.
A rumour behaves like a grass fire in a dry season. One tiny spark -- an overheard remark, an anonymous flyer, a blurry video -- can set whole neighbourhoods of conversation alight. The fire is far easier to start than to put out. Firefighters of the information world do exist: reporters, editors, researchers and careful readers who trace a story back to its source. But their work is slow, and slowness is unpopular.
That is the uncomfortable truth about corrections. A correction is duller than the rumour it chases. It carries no thrill, it asks people to admit they were wrong, and it usually arrives after opinions have already hardened. Studies of online sharing suggest that false stories are passed on far more widely than the corrections that follow them. The rumour gets the crowd; the correction gets a shrug.
Listening plays a part as well. Careless listeners hear half a sentence and repeat a whole story. Each retelling shaves away the doubts and adds certainty the original speaker never claimed. "It might be closed on Friday" becomes "It is closed", and "someone said" becomes "everyone knows". In this way ordinary, honest people become links in a chain of misinformation without ever intending to deceive anyone. The repair is simple but rare: repeat only what you actually heard, and say plainly when you are not sure.
None of this means young people should stop sharing news or lose faith in every message they receive. Communication is a gift, and whole societies run on it. The lesson is smaller and more practical: careful listeners give a story a quiet moment of questioning before they pass it on. They ask where it came from, who benefits, and whether it merely sounds plausible or is actually supported by evidence. They notice when a message seems engineered to produce anger, because anger switches off patient thinking.
The reward for this care is a quality the loudest voices rarely enjoy: trust. A person who checks before speaking may be slower than the crowd, but when that person finally speaks, people listen. Foresight, patience and a habit of questioning cost a few minutes a day. A reputation for telling the truth lasts far longer -- and, once lost, it is very hard to win back.

readings.title: The Fact-Checker's Toolkit
readings.setting: A modern harbour city and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Before you share a story, you can test it. Professional fact-checkers use long checklists and special software, but the heart of their method fits in your pocket: five plain questions that anyone can ask in under five minutes. The simplest definition of misinformation is false information passed on by people who have not checked it. That means every unchecked share, including yours, is part of the machine. Here is the toolkit that switches the machine off.
Question one: who wrote this? Every trustworthy message has an author who is willing to be named. An anonymous message is the weakest kind of source. Nobody puts their name behind the claim, so no one can be questioned or held responsible if it proves false. An honest organiser signs what they share. When a flyer or post refuses to say who made it, treat that silence as information.
Question two: who benefits if I believe it? Ask what the message wants from you: your money, your clicks, your anger, or your attendance at an event. A seller benefits when you panic-buy. An account hungry for followers benefits when you share. Tracing the benefit does not prove a story false, but it tells you whose interests are riding on your belief.
Question three: what is the evidence? A strong story cites sources you can inspect: named witnesses, official statements, documents, dates and figures. A weak story offers only confidence: "everyone knows", "my cousin heard", "they do not want you to find out". If you cannot cite the evidence yourself after reading, then you have not been given any.
Question four: when and where was this made? Old footage wears new captions easily. A video of crates being tipped across a road could come from another country and another year, yet a fresh caption can attach it to your town this afternoon. Shrewd readers check dates, look for landmarks, and search for the original clip before believing the label glued onto it.
Question five: is it plausible when I stop and think? Plausible means the story could be true -- and that is all it means. A conventional trick of hoaxes is to sound just plausible enough that checking feels unnecessary. Slow down and compare the claim with what you already know. If a port were truly closing, would there really be no report anywhere in the news? A single search of two or three trusted outlets settles most panics in less time than it takes to type an apology afterwards.
There is one more rule, and it guards all five questions: notice your own feelings. When a post produces a sudden rush of anger or fear, pause before sharing -- wait, reread and check. Strong feelings are exactly the lever a hoax uses to switch off careful thinking, so the moment you feel most desperate to share is the moment checking matters most.
The toolkit will not dispel every falsehood on the internet, and it will not make you popular with people who prefer excitement to accuracy. What it will do is keep your own name clean. Every time you ask the five questions, you break one link in the chain of misinformation. If enough students in one school build the habit, a hoax that once emptied classrooms cannot even fill a corridor. That is how quiet habits defeat loud lies.

readings.title: Whispers Beyond the Gate, part 1
readings.setting: A modern harbour city and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Amal walked to school just after sunrise. The harbour city shimmered in the early light -- the sea sparkled beyond the rooftops, buses hummed past, and the smell of spiced tea drifted from a corner cafe. It was a temperate morning, mild and pleasant, but something in the air felt strange, like a word caught between the teeth and never quite spoken.
At the school gate, her best friend Nora waved her over. Nora's usually bright expression was clouded, and she dropped her voice to a whisper.
"Have you heard about the embargo?" she asked, eyes wide. "The port is being shut down. No more rice, no fuel, no sugar. People are saying it is going to get very bad very quickly."
Amal blinked. "What? There is nothing about that on the news."
"My cousin Kian told me," Nora explained. "He says he knows someone in customs. He sent a flyer. Look." She pressed a crumpled paper into Amal's hand.
Amal read the bold red letters aloud: "Stand up for our city. Half past three. Harbour Road. Bring signs. Block the trucks. Show your defiance."
There was no organiser's name. No logo. No source. Just urgent words in angry ink. Her gut twisted with doubt.
"And we believe this?" she asked.
Nora bit her lip. "Kian sounded serious. And a protest is happening whether we go or not."
By mid-morning the corridors were buzzing with whispered conversations. Some students scrolled through a short-video app, watching shaky clips of young people tipping crates across a road. The caption read: "We are blocking imports until the leaders hear us. Stand up!"
The rumour was becoming pervasive -- spreading through every classroom, every group chat, every whispered exchange under the stairwell. It seemed as though the entire school believed it.
Amal and Nora sat under the stairwell during break, watching the chaos grow on their screens.
"Is it real?" Nora asked. "Some of it looks staged."
"It could be from anywhere," Amal said carefully. "We do not even know when the video was made. The story seems plausible, but plausible is not the same as true."
"Still," Nora murmured, "if we do nothing, are we just sheep?"
Amal hesitated. "Acting without facts is worse. If we join a lie, we are not helping -- we are hurting."
While Amal was cautious and thoughtful, Nora felt the pull of action. This difference between the two friends would matter as the day unfolded.
In their history lesson, Teacher Yasmin -- calm, precise, and quietly commanding after fifteen years in classrooms -- introduced the vocabulary word foresight.
"Foresight is your ability to see what could happen before it does," she explained, writing the word on the board in careful letters. "It is not about being scared. It is about being wise. A person with foresight asks questions before acting."
Maya raised her hand. "Miss, is not protest a way to stop something bad before it gets worse?"
"Yes," said Teacher Yasmin, "but protest only works when the reason is real and the facts are solid. A conscientious person checks first and acts second."
She turned back to the board. "Let us list examples of productive resistance -- movements that made a real difference -- and then failed ones. Think critically about who had facts and who just followed. I will allot ten minutes for group discussion."
Amal wrote in her notebook: "If we do not think for ourselves, someone else will think for us." She underlined the sentence twice, then sat back, pensive, while the thought of the impending protest pressed on her mind like a storm cloud gathering out over the water.

readings.title: Whispers Beyond the Gate, part 2
readings.setting: A modern harbour city and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
At half past three, Amal and Nora walked down to Harbour Road. They told themselves they were only going to observe, not to participate. But the scene that greeted them was larger and louder than either of them had expected.
Crowds had gathered -- mostly teenagers, some filming on their phones, a few adults watching warily from behind market stalls. Several boys had built a barricade out of fruit crates and old tyres, blocking the road entirely.
"Do not let the trucks pass!" shouted one boy, his voice raw with zeal. "We will not give in!"
Another student with a portable speaker was yelling slogans: "They want us silent! We refuse to be silent!" A few people cheered. Others looked unsure, glancing around as if waiting for someone to tell them what to do.
Amal scanned the crowd with shrewd eyes. Something felt off.
"Look," she pointed. "That boy -- the one with the speaker. He is filming himself, not the protest. He is laughing."
The boy took a selfie in front of the barricade. Another student tagged a post online: "Fake riot for the feed."
"This is a joke," Amal said, jaw tight with frustration. "These people do not care about truth. They want views and followers."
Nora shook her head slowly. "We need to leave. Now."
Although the protest was loud and energetic, it was built on nothing real -- and they both knew it. Behind the barricade, spilt rice and crushed fruit had turned the roadside into a patch of squalor that somebody else would have to clean.
Back at school the next day, the atmosphere had shifted. Where there had been excitement and zeal, there was now embarrassment and silence. A local news outlet had published the truth: "There is no official embargo. A viral student protest has been traced to a hoax flyer. Students were misled."
Teacher Yasmin stood before the class, disappointment etched into her face. The room was so quiet you could hear the ceiling fan turning.
"Who wrote the flyer?" she asked. No one answered.
She sighed. "Then let me ask a different question: what happens when we follow anger instead of truth?"
One boy muttered, "We look stupid."
Amal raised her hand slowly. "We lose trust. People stop believing us -- even when we are telling the truth."
"Exactly," Teacher Yasmin said. "This is not about who started it. It is about what we choose to do next. The revelation that it was a hoax is painful, but it is also an opportunity."
That evening, Nora received a voice message from her cousin Kian -- the same person who had warned her about the embargo in the first place. His voice was shaky: "Nora... I made the flyer. I just wanted to boost my follower count. I thought it would go viral and then everyone would forget. I did not know it would get this serious. I am sorry."
Nora sat frozen, staring at her phone. Then she whispered, "He started all of it."
Amal clenched her fist. "People could have been hurt. There were younger students at that barricade. What if things had turned violent?"
"He was gullible enough to think there would be no consequences," Nora said, her voice edged with dissent from Kian's carelessness. "And we were almost gullible enough to follow him blindly."
"We need to fix this," Amal said. "Somehow."
Nora looked at her, thoughtful now instead of angry. "I think I know how."
The next morning, the two friends pitched an idea to Teacher Yasmin: a weekly Student Forum. There, students could discuss current events, fact-check news, and debate real issues in a respectful environment.
"We want to allot time each week for open dialogue," Amal explained. "A space where people can talk instead of shout, and ask questions instead of following blindly."
Teacher Yasmin studied them for a long moment, then nodded. "You are trying to be part of the solution instead of the problem. I will support this."
At the first meeting, forty students showed up. Some were quiet and nervous. Some were still angry about what had happened. But all of them were curious.

readings.title: Whispers Beyond the Gate, part 3
readings.setting: A modern harbour city and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
"Whereas last week we followed a lie," Amal began, standing in front of the group, "this week we ask questions. That is how real change begins -- not with shouting, but with thinking."
Nora stepped forward. "We need to stop being so gullible. If you cannot cite your facts, do not post them. Do not act on them. Do not share them."
A younger student named Milo spoke up quietly. "Some of us joined the protest out of boredom. We did not think. I feel rueful about that -- genuinely sorry and a little ashamed."
Daniel answered from the back row. "The pressure to act is real. But silence is not always cowardice. Sometimes it is serenity -- choosing to wait, to learn, to understand before you move."
In the weeks that followed, the forum became a safe space for honest discussion. Students learned to assimilate information carefully rather than react to it emotionally. They practised weighing evidence, questioning sources, and respecting viewpoints different from their own. Slowly they began to accustom themselves to a new habit: pausing before believing.
One week they debated censorship. Another week they discussed fairness in school sport, and nobody wasted the hour on a quibble about tiny details of the rules. Then they tackled online disinformation -- the very thing that had started all of this.
Amal moderated a fierce debate about whether protests should be spontaneous or carefully planned.
"Spontaneous actions can change the world," argued Maya. "History is full of moments where people rose up without warning."
"That is true," Nora replied, "but conscientious actions -- ones where people think carefully and prepare -- leave fewer scars. They are slower, yes, but they tend to last. They have longevity."
In the end Maya conceded that planning had won the argument that day, though she promised to keep defending brave beginnings.
A younger student read aloud from a note she had written: "If we do not think for ourselves, someone else will think for us." The next day that line appeared on the wall outside the school in permanent marker. No one knew who had written it, but no one erased it either.
Two months later, a new flyer appeared at the school gates. This one read: "Rise up. Speak loud. Ban school fees for all!"
Some students felt the familiar rush of excitement. Others felt a twinge of recognition -- they had seen this before.
Amal picked up the paper and examined it calmly. She did not rush. She did not react. She smiled.
"All right," she said. "Let us check the source. Who wrote this? Who benefits? What is the data? Is this plausible, or is it another bizarre attempt to manipulate us?"
Instead of rushing into the streets, thirty students joined that week's forum to debate the issue first. They used conventional methods -- research, discussion, evidence -- to investigate the claim, and they pinned a concise summary of what they found to the school noticeboard.
Although the flyer was designed to provoke an immediate reaction, the students responded with foresight and patience. They did not need to dispel rumours with force; they dispelled them with facts.
That was real change. Not loud, not viral -- but lasting.
On the last day of term, Amal and Nora sat on the school rooftop with cups of spiced tea, watching the city stretch below them. The harbour glowed in the late afternoon light, and gulls wheeled and called above the water.
"I am proud of us," Nora said. "We were almost part of a lie. Now we help people question what they hear and think before they act."
Amal nodded. "It is easy to shout. It is harder to think. But thinking is what makes the difference."
Nora smiled. "And thinking lasts longer than shouting."
They sat in comfortable silence, feeling something that did not need a hashtag or a viral video to be real. It was quiet. It was strong. It was the kind of serenity that comes from knowing you chose truth when it would have been easier to follow the crowd.
And in that quiet, they knew: this was just the beginning.

comprehension.question: According to The Speed of a Whisper, what is a rumour, and what are the three reasons the passage gives for why rumours move so fast?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A rumour is a story that runs ahead of its facts, and it moves fast because of excitement, belonging and the sheer speed of modern messages.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored in the opening paragraph and the three numbered reasons of the first information text.

comprehension.question: List the five questions in The Fact-Checker's Toolkit that a careful reader asks before sharing a story.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Who wrote this? Who benefits if I believe it? What is the evidence? When and where was this made? Is it plausible when I stop and think?
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question checking that the learner can locate the five headline questions that structure the toolkit text.

comprehension.question: In part 1 of the story, what does the hoax flyer tell students to do on Harbour Road, and which three details are missing from it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It tells them to bring signs, block the trucks and show their defiance at half past three, but it has no organiser's name, no logo and no source.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored in the flyer scene at the school gate in part 1.

comprehension.question: At the protest in part 2, what does Amal notice about the boy with the portable speaker, and how does another student label the scene online?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She notices that he is filming himself rather than the protest and laughing, and another student tags a post calling it a fake riot for the feed.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored in the moment the protest is exposed as performance in part 2.

comprehension.question: In part 3, why does Milo say he feels rueful, and what does Daniel say silence can sometimes be?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Milo admits that some students joined the protest out of boredom without thinking, and Daniel says silence can sometimes be serenity -- choosing to wait, learn and understand before you move.
comprehension.explanation: An evidence question drawing on the two contrasting confessions at the first forum meeting in part 3.

comprehension.question: The Speed of a Whisper says a rumour behaves like a grass fire in a dry season. What two ideas about rumours does this comparison suggest?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It suggests that one tiny spark can set whole neighbourhoods of conversation alight, and that the fire is far easier to start than to put out.
comprehension.explanation: The learner must interpret figurative language inside an information text and explain the effect of the simile.

comprehension.question: Why does the toolkit call an anonymous message the weakest kind of source?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because nobody puts their name behind the claim, no one can be questioned or held responsible if it proves false, while an honest organiser signs what they share.
comprehension.explanation: An inference-with-evidence question anchored in question one of the toolkit.

comprehension.question: Amal tells Nora that the story seems plausible, but plausible is not the same as true. What does she mean, and how do the two friends differ in part 1?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means a story can sound reasonable and still be false, so it must be checked; Amal wants facts before acting, while Nora feels the pull of action.
comprehension.explanation: A viewpoint question contrasting the two friends' reactions under the stairwell in part 1.

comprehension.question: Teacher Yasmin calls the revelation of the hoax painful, but also an opportunity. Using part 2, explain what was painful and what opportunity it created.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The school felt embarrassment and lost trust after being misled by the fake embargo flyer, but the shock pushed Amal and Nora to propose the weekly Student Forum for fact-checking and respectful debate.
comprehension.explanation: An evaluation question requiring the learner to link the classroom scene to the founding of the forum in part 2.

comprehension.question: How do the students respond to the second flyer about school fees in part 3, and why does the narrator call that response real change?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Thirty students take the flyer to the forum, ask who wrote it and who benefits, and investigate with research, discussion and evidence; it is real change because it is lasting rather than loud or viral.
comprehension.explanation: A synthesis question tracking how the forum's habits transform the school's reaction to the final test in part 3.

comprehension.question: According to The Speed of a Whisper, why does a correction travel more slowly than the rumour it chases, and what do careful listeners give a story before passing it on?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A correction is duller than the rumour, carries no thrill and asks people to admit they were wrong, so careful listeners give a story a quiet moment of questioning first.
comprehension.explanation: A source-reliability question drawing together the corrections paragraph and the closing advice of the first text.

comprehension.question: What does the toolkit advise a reader to do when a post produces a sudden rush of anger or fear, and why?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It advises the reader to pause before sharing -- wait, reread and check -- because strong feelings are exactly the lever a hoax uses to switch off careful thinking.
comprehension.explanation: A critical-evaluation question anchored in the final rule that guards the five toolkit questions.

grammar.title: Contrast Conjunctions: Although, While and Whereas
grammar.explanation: Although, while and whereas are contrast conjunctions: they join two clauses that express different or surprising ideas, showing that both things can be true at the same time even when they seem to conflict.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Although introduces a surprising or unexpected fact, and the clause can open or close the sentence: Although it was raining, the students played outside. She passed the exam although she had not studied much.
While shows that two contrasting things are true at the same time: While Amal preferred careful thinking, Nora wanted to act immediately. While reading is a quiet activity, debating is loud and energetic.
Whereas is more formal and draws a direct comparison between two subjects, usually in the middle of the sentence: The harbour district is crowded and noisy, whereas the old town is quiet. Traditional news is often verified, whereas social media posts may not be checked. Some students showed zeal, whereas others were indifferent.
Punctuation: when the although-clause or while-clause comes first, place a comma before the main clause; when it comes last, no comma is needed.
grammar.commonMistake: Combining although with but, as in: Although it was cold, but we went out. One contrast word per sentence is enough, so write: Although it was cold, we went out. Watch the comma too -- when the although-clause comes first, the comma before the main clause is not optional.
grammar.memoryTip: Although is a door to a surprise, while is two paths running side by side, and whereas is a spotlight shining on the difference between two things.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- fill each blank with although, while or whereas: 1) ______ the exam was easy, many students still made mistakes. 2) ______ I enjoy football, my friend prefers basketball. 3) Cats are independent, ______ dogs need more attention. 4) ______ it was very noisy outside, she managed to concentrate. 5) He speaks three languages, ______ his brother speaks only one. 6) ______ both teams played well, only one could win.
Part B -- combine each pair using the word in brackets: 7) It was a holiday. The shops were closed. (although) 8) Maya likes Science. Leo prefers English. (whereas) 9) The weather was hot. The students wore jackets. (although) 10) Some people trust social media. Others prefer newspapers. (while)
Check your answers with your teacher or AI tutor before moving on.

grammar.title: -ing Forms as Subjects and Objects
grammar.explanation: When you add -ing to a verb and use it as a noun, it is called a gerund; gerunds can be the subject of a sentence or the object that follows verbs such as enjoy, avoid, finish and practise.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
As a subject, the -ing form opens the sentence and names the activity being discussed: Reading improves your vocabulary. Citing evidence makes your argument stronger. Thinking critically is an essential life skill.
As an object, the -ing form follows verbs such as enjoy, like, love, hate, avoid, finish, practise and suggest: I enjoy reading before bed. He avoids quibbling about small details. They finished studying for the test.
Do not confuse gerunds with the present continuous. In She is reading a book, the -ing form is part of the verb phrase with is; in Reading is her favourite hobby, the activity itself is the subject and works as a noun.
grammar.commonMistake: Labelling every -ing word as the continuous tense. In They are preparing for the debate, preparing follows are and describes an action in progress, but in I dislike waiting in long queues, waiting is a gerund object -- there is no am, is or are in front of it.
grammar.memoryTip: If you can put the phrase 'the activity of' in front of the -ing word and the sentence still makes sense, you are looking at a gerund, not a tense.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- say whether each -ing form is a gerund used as subject, a gerund used as object, or part of the present continuous: 1) Jogging every morning keeps me healthy. 2) They are preparing for the debate. 3) I dislike waiting in long queues. 4) Learning new words is exciting. 5) She is writing an essay. 6) He practises speaking English every day.
Part B -- complete each sentence with the -ing form of the verb in brackets: 7) ______ (cook) is a useful life skill. 8) I enjoy ______ (listen) to podcasts in English. 9) ______ (spread) rumours can destroy friendships. 10) She avoids ______ (argue) about politics. 11) ______ (assimilate) into a new culture takes time.

grammar.title: The Present Continuous Tense
grammar.explanation: The present continuous describes actions happening right now or currently in progress, using am, is or are plus the -ing form, and it gives writing a feeling of immediacy and movement.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + am, is or are + verb-ing. I am studying; you, we and they are studying; he, she and it is studying.
Spelling rules for adding -ing: most verbs add -ing directly (talk becomes talking); verbs ending in -e drop the e (make becomes making, argue becomes arguing); short consonant-vowel-consonant verbs double the final letter (run becomes running, sit becomes sitting); verbs ending in -ie change ie to y (lie becomes lying).
Examples in context: The students are whispering in the corridors. Nora is reading the flyer carefully. People are shouting slogans at the protest. Amal is thinking about whether the rumour is true. The forum members are learning to question information.
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping the helper verb or mismatching it with the subject, as in They studying for the exam or We is discussing the topic. The tense always needs the right form of be: They are studying, and We are discussing. Spelling slips such as argueing for arguing are the other frequent trap.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of am, is and are plus -ing as a live broadcast: the camera is rolling on the action at this very moment.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- rewrite each sentence in the present continuous: 1) She writes in her journal. 2) They discuss the problem. 3) He plans the next meeting. 4) We learn new vocabulary. 5) The teacher explains the rule.
Part B -- correct the mistake in each sentence: 6) She is argueing with her friend. 7) They studying for the exam. 8) He am reading a book. 9) We is discussing the topic. 10) I are writing an essay.

grammar.title: Abstract Nouns
grammar.explanation: Abstract nouns name ideas, qualities, emotions and states that you cannot see, touch or measure with your senses -- this unit's examples include serenity, foresight, dissent, zeal, defiance, revelation and longevity.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Many abstract nouns are built from adjectives or verbs: calm becomes serenity, defy becomes defiance, reveal becomes revelation, and long becomes longevity; dissent works as both verb and noun, and a person who dissents is a dissenter.
Pair abstract nouns with fitting verbs: you feel serenity, show foresight, express dissent and demonstrate zeal.
Good: She felt a deep serenity watching the sunset. Awkward: She held the serenity in her hands -- serenity is not an object you can hold.
Using abstract nouns lifts your writing: instead of he planned ahead, write he showed great foresight; instead of she was very enthusiastic, write her zeal was inspiring.
grammar.commonMistake: Treating an abstract noun like a physical object, as in He picked up his courage from the table, or muddling near-neighbours: dissent is disagreement you express, whereas defiance is refusal to obey -- the forum welcomed dissent, but blocking the road was defiance.
grammar.memoryTip: Try the camera test: you can photograph a barricade, but no camera can photograph zeal, foresight or serenity -- if the lens cannot catch it, the noun is abstract.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- name the abstract noun in each sentence: 1) His foresight in saving money helped the family during the crisis. 2) The student showed great zeal when presenting her project. 3) There was growing dissent among the students about the new policy. 4) After the argument, a sense of serenity returned to the classroom. 5) The revelation shocked the entire school.
Part B -- fill each blank with serenity, foresight, defiance, zeal, revelation or dissent: 6) She approached her studies with great ______ and never missed a deadline. 7) The ______ that the flyer was a hoax surprised everyone. 8) His ______ in planning ahead saved the project from failure. 9) The community expressed their ______ against the unfair decision. 10) After a stressful week, she found ______ in reading by the sea.

grammar.title: Reported Speech
grammar.explanation: Reported speech lets you tell someone what another person said without quoting the exact words, shifting tenses one step back and adjusting pronouns and time expressions to fit the new sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Tense shifts: present simple becomes past simple (I study becomes she studied); present continuous becomes past continuous (I am studying becomes she was studying); past simple becomes past perfect (I studied becomes she had studied); will becomes would and can becomes could.
Pronouns and time words change too: I becomes he or she, my becomes his or her, today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, here becomes there, and now becomes then.
Statements: He said, "I am happy." becomes He said that he was happy. Questions: She asked, "Are you ready?" becomes She asked if I was ready; He asked, "Where is the meeting?" becomes He asked where the meeting was. Commands: She said, "Close the door." becomes She told me to close the door.
grammar.commonMistake: Reporting a question with question-mark word order, as in She asked where was the meeting. Once the question is reported, the clause returns to statement order: She asked where the meeting was, with no question mark and no repeated helper verb.
grammar.memoryTip: When the quotation marks disappear, the tense takes one step back into the past -- picture the words stepping backwards out of the speech bubble.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- convert each sentence to reported speech: 1) Amal said, "I do not believe the rumour." 2) Nora said, "My cousin sent me a flyer." 3) Teacher Yasmin asked, "Who wrote the flyer?" 4) Maya said, "I will check the facts before I share anything." 5) Milo said, "I joined the protest out of boredom." 6) Daniel asked, "Are you coming to the forum meeting?"
Part B -- convert each reported sentence back to direct speech: 7) She said that she was feeling proud of the forum. 8) He told me that he would attend the next meeting. 9) The teacher asked if we had finished reading the story.

grammar.title: Conditionals, Connectives and Multi-Word Verbs
grammar.explanation: This lesson gathers three tools for reasoning aloud: the zero conditional for facts, the first conditional for real future possibilities, five connectives that link ideas logically, and the multi-word verbs give in, carry out and speak up.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Zero conditional, for things that are always true: If + present simple, present simple. If you heat ice, it melts. If people spread rumours, trust decreases.
First conditional, for likely futures: If + present simple, will + base verb. If Amal checks the source, she will discover the truth. If the forum meets next week, thirty students will attend.
Connectives and their jobs: because gives a reason (I stayed home because I was ill); so that gives a purpose (She studied hard so that she could pass); although concedes a contrast (Although it rained, we went outside); however signals an unexpected turn (I was tired; however, I finished my work); therefore draws a conclusion (He lied; therefore, he lost our trust).
Multi-word verbs: give in means to stop resisting (He finally gave in and apologised); carry out means to perform or complete (They carried out the investigation); speak up means to express your opinion or talk louder (Do not be afraid to speak up).
grammar.commonMistake: Slipping will into the if-clause, as in If it will rain, we will stay inside; the if-clause stays in the present simple, so write If it rains, we will stay inside. With connectives, remember that however needs a semicolon or full stop before it, not just a comma.
grammar.memoryTip: Zero conditional equals zero doubt, first conditional looks at the future first; connectives are road signs between ideas, and in a multi-word verb the little particle steers the meaning.
grammar.practice:
Part A -- label each sentence zero or first conditional: 1) If you do not water plants, they die. 2) If she finishes early, she will help us. 3) If you press this button, the machine starts. 4) If we fact-check the news, we will avoid spreading lies. 5) If it snows, the roads become slippery.
Part B -- complete with the correct verb forms: 6) If you ______ (not check) the facts, you ______ (believe) lies. (zero) 7) If Nora ______ (attend) the meeting, she ______ (share) her ideas. (first) 8) If students ______ (think) critically, they ______ (make) better decisions. (zero) 9) If the rain ______ (stop), we ______ (go) to the park. (first)
Part C -- join each pair with the connective in brackets: 10) She was tired. She stayed up to study. (although) 11) He checked the facts. He could give an accurate report. (so that) 12) The evidence was clear. The committee changed its decision. (therefore) 13) The protest seemed real. It was actually a hoax. (however) 14) Students joined the forum. They wanted to learn critical thinking. (because)
Part D -- complete with give in, carry out or speak up: 15) If you disagree with something, you should ______. 16) The students will ______ a survey on misinformation. 17) After hours of discussion, the committee decided to ______ to the students' demands. 18) Please ______ so that everyone at the back can hear you. 19) The team was asked to ______ the plan exactly as discussed.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Contrast Debate
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Choose one of these motions and prepare a two-minute speech that uses at least two contrast conjunctions (although, while, whereas): social media helps learning although it can also spread false information; traditional news sources are checked by editors, whereas online posts are often unverified; spontaneous protests raise awareness quickly, while planned campaigns usually last longer. Structure your speech with an opening statement of your position, two supporting points that acknowledge the other side through a contrast conjunction, and a conclusion that restates your view in one strong closing sentence. Model line: "Although a viral post reaches thousands in minutes, a checked report earns something rarer -- trust." Practise with your AI tutor or a classmate before recording.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Help me practise contrast debate and give feedback on clarity, vocabulary, evidence, reasoning and audience effect.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Retelling in Reported Speech
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Choose three scenes from Whispers Beyond the Gate and retell each one in reported speech, changing tenses, pronouns and time expressions correctly. Model lines: Nora told Amal that there was going to be a protest on Harbour Road. She explained that her cousin had sent a flyer. Amal replied that the story seemed plausible but that plausible was not the same as true. Retell the flyer scene, the confession and the second flyer, then record the retelling you are proudest of.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Help me practise retelling in reported speech and give feedback on clarity, vocabulary, evidence, reasoning and audience effect.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Discussion Circle
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Hold a discussion circle with classmates or during your teacher session. Use full sentences, support every opinion with a reason, and listen respectfully when others speak. Discuss these four questions: Is it ever right to join a protest if you are not completely sure about the facts? How can young people tell the difference between real news and misinformation? The story shows that silence can sometimes be a strength -- do you agree, and can you give an example? What responsibilities do social media users have when they share information online?

writing.title: Writing 1: Opinion Essay on Spotting Misinformation
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write an opinion essay of 200 to 250 words answering this question: should students be taught how to identify misinformation as part of their school curriculum? Open with an introduction of two or three sentences that states your opinion. In body paragraph one, give your first reason with an example and include one contrast conjunction. In body paragraph two, give your second reason and use reported speech to reference something a person in this unit said. Close with a conclusion of two or three sentences that summarises your view and ends on a strong final statement. Use connectives to link your ideas and include at least two abstract nouns.
writing.modelText: Although some adults believe young people cannot be fooled, the hoax in this unit proves otherwise. Teacher Yasmin said that protest only works when the facts are solid, and a curriculum that teaches source-checking would give every student that foresight before the next flyer appears.

writing.title: Writing 2: Contrast Paragraph: Communication Then and Now
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write one paragraph of 120 to 150 words comparing how people communicated in the past with how they communicate today. Begin with a topic sentence that states your main idea. In your supporting sentences, contrast letters, face-to-face conversation and radio with instant messaging, video calls and social media, using at least two contrast conjunctions (although, while, whereas). Work in at least three vocabulary words from the unit list -- for example, gullible readers, conventional sources or greater foresight. Finish with a concluding sentence about what this change means for the future.
writing.modelText: Communication has changed dramatically over the past century. Whereas a letter once crossed the sea in weeks, a message now arrives before the writer has finished thinking. While conventional newspapers employed editors to check every claim, today's feeds reward speed, and gullible readers pay the price.

activities.title: Activities 1: Contrast Conjunction Workout
activities.instructionsAndItems: Fill each blank with although, while or whereas, then rewrite two of the sentences with the clause order reversed: 1) ______ Maya prefers reading fiction, her brother enjoys non-fiction books. 2) ______ the weather was very hot, the students continued their outdoor activity. 3) The harbour district is busy and loud, ______ the old town stays quiet. 4) ______ some people believe everything they read online, others are more sceptical. 5) She worked very hard on the project, ______ the final result was disappointing. 6) Traditional markets are lively and social, ______ online shopping is convenient but impersonal. 7) ______ the exam was difficult, most students managed to pass. 8) Daniel likes to plan everything in advance, ______ Maya is more spontaneous.

activities.title: Activities 3: Vocabulary Detective
activities.instructionsAndItems: Round one -- match each word to its definition: 1) embargo, 2) pensive, 3) shrewd, 4) concede, 5) spontaneous, 6) pervasive, 7) longevity, 8) squalor.
